description: No fixed number, but a practical answer: which words recur in 11+ English papers, how many a Year 4-5 child needs, and how to prioritise.

sections.heading: There is no official word count
paragraphs: No 11+ board publishes a vocabulary list, and anyone selling you an exact number is guessing. the main paper styles and school-written papers all draw on the same broad school vocabulary, and what separates strong candidates is not rare words but fast, confident handling of ordinary ones under time pressure.

Think in bands rather than totals. A Year 4 child heading for the 11+ typically needs the everyday band secure first: common words used precisely, then the less-common band where most lost marks live — words like reluctant, frugal or vivid that adults use without thinking and children misread under pressure.

sections.heading: Why the same words keep appearing
paragraphs: Examiners favour words with clear synonyms and antonyms, because those make clean multiple-choice questions. That is why the same few thousand words recur year after year: they are testable, not fashionable. A child who knows them handles synonyms, antonyms, cloze and odd-one-out questions with the same knowledge.

This recurrence is good news. It means vocabulary preparation converges: the words worth learning for a Kent paper are overwhelmingly the same words worth learning for a Buckinghamshire or London independent paper.

sections.heading: How many is enough, practically
paragraphs: As a working rule, aim for roughly two thousand words known well rather than five thousand half-known. Known well means the child can give the meaning, pick the synonym and the antonym, and use the word in a sentence of their own. A word that only survives as a memorised definition will not survive a timed paper.

Count in both directions. Words learned but never revisited fade within weeks, so the total that matters is words retained, not words covered. Short lists with regular recycling beat long lists done once.

sections.heading: Where to find the words
paragraphs: Start with what the child already reads: pull unfamiliar words from school books and library reads into a running list, a dozen a week at most. Then add a curated exam-word list for coverage, so the less-common band does not arrive as a surprise in September of Year 6.

Free GL familiarisation papers show the formats the words appear in, which matters as much as the words themselves. A word practised only as a definition is a different skill from the same word tested as a synonym under time pressure.

standfirst: Nobody can give you an exact number, but examiners reuse the same testable words — so preparation converges on roughly two thousand words known well.
title: How Many Words Does My Child Need for the 11+?
